item.title: Public Speaking Anxiety: A 5-Step Approach
item.description:
Coaching

Public Speaking Anxiety: A 5-Step Approach

Working with a performance psychiatrist can help you build a mental edge.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • Working with a performance psychiatrist gives executives access to the same mental tools elite athletes use.
  • A five-part approach includes goal setting, CBT, visualization, emotional regulation, and strategy.
  • These strategies are based on performance research.
Source: Wavebreakmedia/iStockPhoto

Several years ago, the CEO of a large financial company referred a high-performing partner to me to improve his presentation skills for a large conference. Let's call him Nathan*. He was a 45-year-old, experienced speaker who had given many presentations and conferences throughout his career. The CEO knew about my work as a performance psychiatrist who works with professional athletes and executives.

For three months, his stress was mounting. He was convinced he would shake in front of the audience and that the presentation would flop. The more he thought about it, the more anxious he became. By the time we met, the presentation was occupying his mind day and night. It was beginning to interfere with his other work. The conference was still a few months away, so we had time to address the challenges.

My approach to performance psychiatry is individualized, but five elements are essential to how I work with people who want to perform at a high level.

Goal Setting

The first is goal setting. Research shows that specific, measurable goals increase motivation and "task performance." Nathan initially said he wanted to stop being anxious, but anxiety is a normal part of high-level performance and is not always within our control, although it can be reduced. Together, we set a more useful goal: "I feel confident, enthusiastic, composed, and fulfilled while giving my presentation at the Annual Conference, working five hours a week on this preparation and practice, following my strategy, and keeping track of the mental performance strategies I learn." The goal was never to eliminate fear. It was to help him perform effectively, even when anxiety was present.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Self-Talk

The second element is based on cognitive behavioral therapy, which focuses on the interaction between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. We discussed the automatic thoughts driving Nathan's fear. Some of these thoughts included "People will notice that I am trembling," "I shouldn't be nervous—I'm a leader and executive," and "I will embarrass myself." We examined the evidence for and against these fears and worked through worst-case, best-case, and most-likely scenarios. We also practiced realistic self-talk, which differs from positive thinking. Nathan used short, evidence-based phrases such as "This is practice" and "I did the work," and repeated them during preparation and on the morning of the event.

Visualization

The third element is visualization, or the mental practice of a behavior. Nathan and I visualized every stage of the presentation, from entering the room to clearly communicating his message, and described it aloud in the present tense. We kept it realistic, rather than imagining a flawless, fear-free performance, and he practiced noticing fear as he continued to speak. We recorded five different visualizations, and he listened to them twice a day.

Emotional Regulation

The fourth element is emotional regulation. When Nathan became overwhelmed, he started imagining worst-case scenarios. I taught him mindful breathing, inhaling through the nose and exhaling longer than the inhale, which can trigger a calming response, along with grounding techniques that bring attention back to the present. He found labeling particularly helpful. Rather than saying "I'm anxious," he would say "Oh...anxiety is here." Research suggests that labeling emotions in this way can reduce activity in the amygdala. The goal was never to make the fear go away. It was to notice it, regulate the reaction, and refocus on the task at hand.

Detailed Strategy

The fifth element, and one of the most important, is creating a detailed, written strategy. We made a plan for when and how often Nathan would practice, and what he should focus on at each stage. We continued with the visualizations. He also practiced the presentation out loud. Research supports that the more practice resembles the real event, the better. The goal wasn't to memorize the presentation. The goal was to become very comfortable executing under pressure.

By the time of the conference, Nathan and I had met for 10 sessions. He still felt nervous as the date got closer, but he now had strategies for working with it, and he understood that some fear was normal and not a sign that something was wrong. On the day of the presentation, he was better prepared than ever before. It went well. The delivery wasn't perfect, and that was fine. After that, he felt proud, both of how it had gone and of everything he had learned.

This is the work I do with executives and athletes who want to perform at their best under pressure. Fear rarely disappears completely, but with the right approach, it doesn't have to take the lead.

*Disclaimer: Nathan is not a real client. Details in this document, including identifying information, have been amended to ensure confidentiality.

item.title: The Frustration You Can't Explain
item.description:
Guilt

The Frustration You Can't Explain

Frustration is a signal, and it's usually pointing at someone you're protecting.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • Frustration is a signal pointing to blocked, hidden ambitions; it's not just a mood to be managed.
  • Beliefs formed in childhood often block ambition to unconsciously protect loved ones.
  • Naming ambitions and their objections helps expose and loosen deeply rooted limiting beliefs.

If you're frustrated with your life, something specific is in hiding. Something is blocked, and you can't quite see it. It's not a vague dissatisfaction—it's a particular thing you want to be doing and aren't.

Frustration is usually treated as a mood, something to be managed or waited out. It isn't. It's a signal, and it's precise. People who don't want anything don't feel frustrated. They feel flat, or bored, or blandly content. Frustration requires an obstructed aim.

The trouble is that most of us can't say what we're wanting to do, or to make, or to be. We've concealed it — first from other people, and then, with time, from ourselves.

Ambition is the thing we learn to conceal

Most of us weren't raised to show open ambition. Women especially, though not infrequently men as well. At 3 or 4 years old, or later, someone warned us that wanting to be successful invited danger. Open ambition is risky; it invites envy, ridicule, or disappointment in the people you love and who love you. So whatever fantastic dreaming we did as small children, we learned to send those images underground.

What remains is a set of expectations about what will happen if we pursue the things we want. Some predict failure. But the more powerful ones predict something else: that if we succeed, someone we love will be hurt.

These are called pathogenic beliefs—from pathos, suffering, and -genic, giving rise to. These are beliefs that produce the trouble. They form early, out of childhood experience, and they aren't ideas we consciously remember. They sit below awareness, and they're almost never about self-interest. They're warnings about harm coming to someone else.

There's a second thing about these beliefs that matters. What the child observed was usually accurate. The father did erupt. The mother was left alone. The brother really did struggle. The error is in the causal arithmetic. Small children put themselves at the center of everything because they can't yet see that the adults around them have lives of their own. So the child concludes: I caused this. It's a misattribution, and it's a protective one. If it's my fault, then my father isn't cruel, and my mother isn't leaving for reasons of her own.

Here's what that looks like. Your father ran off with another woman when you were small, and your mother never had anything like love again. Years later, you fall in love with a wonderful man, and you can't stop expecting him to leave. You believe that if you tell him how you feel, he'll walk away and you'll never see him again. Underneath, hidden from you, is loyalty to your mother. You feel disloyal imagining a happy ending because it would make her suffer by comparison. So you say goodbye to him without ever letting him know you adore him.

Who gets left behind

This is the part that gets missed in most discussions of blocked ambition. We're told we're afraid of failure. We're reminded that we're sabotaging ourselves—meaning we're to blame. We're the criminal and the victim, all at once.

In my clinical experience, and in the research my colleagues and I have done over three decades, the more common fear is of surpassing others. It's survivor guilt, and it's sitting on our secret ambitions, hiding under the rocks and in the closets we all live with.

A woman whose mother had no career of her own can't quite finish her dissertation. A man from a family where nobody ever left town finds he can't accept the job offer in another city; he can't explain why, and says he's afraid of failing. A girl whose brother could never do his homework can't bring her report card home to her family and eventually can't let herself thrive at anything.

None of this is conscious. What's conscious is the frustration, the stalling, the sense of being stuck in glue. What's underneath is loyalty.

The belief usually sounds something like: If I have this, someone I love will be diminished by comparison. Or: my having more means they had less. Survivor guilt is one of the most reliable predictors of depression we've found.

Your ambitions are only aimed at what's possible

This is something reassuring that I know to be true and have never seen disproven in the consulting room.

You will not find yourself longing to be an Olympic gymnast at 60. You won't ache to be a composer if you're tone deaf. You won't yearn to be a mathematician if you've hated math since fourth grade.

The mind is adaptive. It doesn't generate desires for the impossible. This means that whatever you actually want—the thing you've concealed, the thing you'd be embarrassed to say out loud or write down—is something you have some real capacity for. That's why it occurred to you.

You may not get it. Circumstances intervene. But the wanting itself is evidence.

What to do about it

You can't simply decide to feel differently. And you can't change an old belief because someone tells you it's mistaken. If that worked, therapy would take an afternoon.

Beliefs change through experience. You take an action, and then you wait to see what happens. The waiting is usually full of anxiety—a jittery stomach, maybe sweating. And when the catastrophe you predicted doesn't arrive, you breathe out, and you might even feel happy.

But first the beliefs have to be identified, and they only surface when you imagine doing the thing you were warned about.

So, sit down somewhere private—very private—and make a list of what you want. Include all of it, the large ambitions and the small ones, especially the ones you'd be mortified to have anyone see. Don't be realistic. Realism is where the beliefs are already doing their work.

Then, as you write, pay attention to the objections arriving. They come fast, they feel like reasonable considerations, and every one of them carries a warning:

  • Who am I to think I could do that?
  • I'd have to neglect my family.
  • People would think I was full of myself.
  • My mother would never have done this.

Write those down too, in a separate list. That's the real document. Those sentences are the beliefs, and they've been operating on you for decades without ever being read aloud.

Then pick one ambition and take the first concrete step toward it—a small one, this week.

What usually happens

The frustration recedes, not because you've achieved anything yet, but because the aim is out in the open. You've stopped running into a wall you couldn't see.

And more often than not, the person you thought you were protecting turns out not to need protecting. This isn't because the danger was imaginary—often, it wasn't—but because you were never its cause. That's the discovery that changes things: You have been running a calculation you made at the age of 5, on evidence you may have read correctly, but with the arrow pointing the wrong way.

Your success, when it comes, does not diminish the people you love. More often it frees them.

item.title: Reframing Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
item.description:
Chronic Illness

Reframing Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension

A case for optimism during IIH Awareness Month.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • September is IIH Awareness Month, honoring those diagnosed with idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
  • Optimism, gratitude, and meaning-making were as vital to healing as the surgery itself.

It seems that every cause has a designated day or month to raise awareness for that individual ailment. Well, September is upon us, and it is designated as IIH Awareness Month. Thirty days to recognize those diagnosed with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and their journey towards recovery. Like many of you, this campaign did not mean anything to me in the years past, and I had never even heard of IIH. Times have changed, and in March of 2025, I found myself becoming an expert through my own diagnosis of this rare disease. IIH is not something you are at risk of dying from, but it is something you are challenged to live with. From headaches to tinnitus and nausea to loss of vision, those managing IIH need to stay on top of their health to maintain a high quality of life.

Let’s talk a bit about what IIH is and who it is likely to affect

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is defined exactly as it reads. Idiopathic means there is no specific reason why you may have this problem. Intracranial translates to in your head. Hypertension refers to high pressure caused by fluid retention.

Essentially, your body has produced an excess of cerebrospinal fluid that is now trapped between your skull and brain rather than draining properly through the sinus veins and back into your circulatory system. You may now be asking yourself why this happens. Well, that takes us back to the first “I”; we have no idea. So how is this treated, and what are the effects of the disease?

First, let’s understand who this disease affects

The literature shows that only a few percent at most of those affected are men. Cases of IIH are predominantly seen in women ages 19-24 who are significantly overweight. For those who know me, I don’t self-identify as any of those categories. I am a 51-year-old man (49 at diagnosis) who is physically fit and very active. I am an avid cyclist, hiker, and skier, and I spend five to six days a week in the gym. Needless to say, I was quite surprised by my diagnosis.

My symptoms started with a loss of peripheral vision in my right eye, and within five days, I was looking through pinholes in both my eyes even as my visual acuity remained sharp. By the time I saw the ophthalmologist, I was contending with an unbearable headache, profuse sweating, and persistent nausea. A digital scan revealed significant swelling in both optic nerves.

The doctor shared the troubling news that I was suffering from either brain swelling or a brain tumor and coordinated an immediate transfer to the hospital. My mom died of a brain tumor at 54 years old, so I was convinced of my own fate. I had no hope or optimism and was unable to care for my most basic needs. I was willing myself to die.

After nearly three weeks and two hospitals, I learned that I did not have a brain tumor and that this middle-aged, athletic male was diagnosed with a young, heavy girl’s disease. It took me some time to process that too. Over the two weeks, I transitioned from certain and hopeful death to an optimist who had reframed his situation, going from why did this happen to me to why did this happen for me.

I was very lucky. I was diagnosed early. I was able to be seen by a leading neuro-ophthalmologist in one of the world’s preeminent IIH facilities (Hospital at the University of Pennsylvania). I was then operated on by the world’s leading neurovascular surgeon for the required procedure. I had every opportunity to effectively treat my disease and the related symptoms.

While we will never know what caused the increase in CSF production that led to my diagnosis, we did learn why the buildup could not resolve itself. My transverse sinus veins are anything but equal; specifically, the left side does 10 percent of the drainage while the right does 90 percent. The right was found to have a significant stenosis causing a near-complete blockage. The intervention was to stent the right side and straighten the stenosis to open up the drain.

The fix was instant; the symptoms began an immediate reversal, and after 72 hours I was stabilized. The vision in my left eye went back to 100 percent, my right eye 77 percent, and all other symptoms were resolved. I am certainly very fortunate.

However, the stent was not the only intervention. Dr. Mary Seligman argues in Flourish (2011) that therapeutic interventions constitute only one component of recovery; optimism and positive orientation are equally as important. I was determined to get back to 100 percent. Back to biking, hiking, skiing, and living a fulfilled and good life.

I had hope and optimism, a solid support system, and a documented set of achievements toward my recovery goals. I used many positive psychology interventions to get there. From gratitude and grit to finding meaning and being my best possible self at every stage of recovery. In the end, it was optimism that healed my mind, body, and soul.

We will all encounter hard moments in our lives, and a health crisis may represent the most demanding test of a person’s whole self. I tell my children that we are equipped to do hard things and that they need to see themselves as victors rather than victims. By staying focused and putting one foot in front of the other with intention and purpose, we can always find our way forward. Viktor Frankl wrote (1959/2006), “He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.” He went on to say, “When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.” This is what the fight for well-being looks like.

So as we recognize IIH this September, let’s honor those who live as victors and have found strength through their adversity, while finding ways to lift up those who are still in search of meaning and their own well-being. Stay resilient and earn your badge every day!

item.title: Ozempic, Anhedonia, and the Brain’s Reward System
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

Ozempic, Anhedonia, and the Brain’s Reward System

GLP-1 medications may change more than just appetite.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • Some people report feeling emotionally flat after starting GLP-1 medications.
  • GLP-1 medications affect neural pathways involved in reward, not appetite alone.
  • Clinical trials show overall mental health improves on GLP-1s, despite some reports of anhedonia.
Source: David Trinks / Unsplash

Some people taking GLP-1 medications describe a change that goes beyond eating less. Food occupies their thoughts less often, and they may notice less interest in activities they previously enjoyed.

They may not feel sad or depressed, but describe themselves as emotionally flat or indifferent.

This experience has been called the “Ozempic personality” or the “meh effect,” although neither term is a medical diagnosis. Because GLP-1 medications affect brain systems involved in reward and motivation as well as appetite, some researchers and clinicians have considered whether these reports could involve anhedonia, a diminished capacity to experience pleasure. That possibility is still far from established, particularly because the changes reported by patients vary considerably.

The Brain’s Reward System

GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide are primarily discussed in terms of appetite, digestion, and blood glucose. But GLP-1 signaling also interacts with neural circuits involved in reward.

Research suggests that these medications change the brain’s response to food-related cues, particularly highly palatable foods. A 2024 systematic review found consistent effects on reward-related behavior, although their precise mechanisms remain unclear.

To understand how GLP-1 medications may affect reward, it helps to distinguish between wanting and liking. Wanting is the motivational drive to seek a reward, while liking refers to the pleasure experienced when the reward is obtained.

This distinction is relevant because reducing food-related wanting can be therapeutic when cravings contribute to overeating. It becomes more complicated when changes in motivation are no longer specific to food, particularly if activities that were previously rewarding also become less appealing.

The Effect Is Not Just Psychological

The effects of GLP-1 medications on reward are not simply psychological reactions to eating less or losing weight. GLP-1 receptors are found in brain regions involved in motivation and reward, and GLP-1 signaling can affect neural pathways that regulate dopamine and other processes involved in how rewards are valued.

This provides a biological basis for some of the changes people describe after starting semaglutide. The medication can alter how the brain processes the motivational value of food, rather than simply making a person decide to eat less.

What remains uncertain is whether these effects can extend beyond food to produce broader changes in motivation or pleasure.

Other Possible Causes of Anhedonia Should Be Considered

Anhedonia can have several possible causes, including other medications, substance use, sleep disturbances, neurological conditions, and changes in physical health. These factors can affect the brain’s reward and motivation systems independently of GLP-1 treatment.

This becomes important when anhedonia appears after starting semaglutide. A symptom that begins during treatment may be related to the medication, but it may also have another cause that emerged around the same time.

The timing alone therefore cannot establish that semaglutide is responsible.

GLP-1s Often Improve Mental Health

Despite reports of emotional flattening or reduced interest among some people taking GLP-1 medications, clinical studies have generally found improvements in mental health during treatment.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 80 randomized clinical trials involving more than 107,000 participants found that GLP-1 receptor agonists were associated with better mental health-related quality of life, without an increased risk of psychiatric adverse events.

This does not make individual reports of anhedonia less real. It does, however, place them in the context of what has been observed across much larger groups of patients. A person may experience a reduction in pleasure or motivation while the average participant in a clinical trial experiences an improvement in psychological well-being.

The two findings are therefore not necessarily contradictory, since clinical trials describe what tends to happen across a population, while individual reports can reveal effects that are less common or that are not captured by the measures used in those trials.

item.title: 5 Key Steps to Overcoming the Happiness Paradox
item.description:
Happiness

5 Key Steps to Overcoming the Happiness Paradox

A recent study unlocks how to achieve genuine happiness without forcing it.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • Studies of happiness suggest it's harder to feel happy the more you try—the so-called paradox of happiness.
  • Breaking the pursuit of happiness into components can help separate the pitfalls from the promises.
  • Understanding what can contribute to happiness can bring not only greater joy, but more fulfillment.

As a general rule, most people would rather be happy than unhappy. The trick is to figure out how to maximize the pleasure-pain ratio.

According to the so-called “paradox of happiness,” the more you seek happiness, the more elusive it becomes. How, then, can you get to your desired outcome without falling prey to this impossibility?

Unpacking the Paradox of Happiness

In a recent thought-provoking review, University of Berkeley’s Iris Mauss and University of Toronto’s Brett Ford (2026) address the happiness paradox, noting that the “pursuit of happiness is a human universal with a mixed track record." Consistent with the tenets of positive psychology, sometimes it’s better to focus on your situation at the moment, flaws and all, rather than try to force out an unnatural sense of joy.

You can probably relate to this if you think back on a day when you had high hopes for how things would go. Out with a group of your favorite people, you sit down for what you expect to be a “perfect” evening. You want to be happy, but within moments of the event getting underway, someone makes an annoying comment. Suddenly, you’re embroiled in a very unpleasant debate, and it all goes downhill from there. If only you could push rewind and start all over again. You wouldn’t let that comment detract from your mood.

Mauss and Ford believe that it is precisely because people strive for happiness that they become led into the very opposite set of emotions. Letting happiness flow over a situation without forcing it should be far more effective. They suggest doing this requires breaking down the pursuit of happiness into parts.

5 Steps in the Path to Happiness

As laid out in their theoretical model, you can reach the desired outcome of happiness by going through these five steps:

  1. Setting a happiness goal. Happiness-related strivings, such as agreeing with the statement, “I try very hard to be happy,” needn’t set you up for failure. The problem isn’t aspiring to happiness; it’s what you do to reach that goal that can create misery.
  2. Affect regulation. Happiness is, “at its core,” an affective state, note the authors. In affect regulation, you adjust your affect to align your current state with the goal. Sometimes you have to turn things up and at other times turn them down. One important way to do this is through cognitive change. Sure, this person said something that irked you, but was it meant to be annoying? Maybe there was a legitimate basis for the misunderstanding. Convincing yourself that the remark was intended to be mean will only bring you down, so instead look for a possible saving grace.
  3. Monitoring. Think about and reflect on how you are actually feeling. Quoting Socrates, who noted that “the unexamined life is not worth living,*” the authors suggest that while you can overthink your emotions, maybe you can benefit from savoring the moment. Look around at the people with you who, by definition, you care for and enjoy. Letting that remark slide can get you back to a position of enjoying these particular individuals. Importantly, the authors suggest that monitoring your affect can help you determine whether you are in fact on track to achieve your happiness goal.
  4. Responding. Now you’re in a position to judge your happiness. Maybe everything isn’t perfect. Well, that’s okay. Consistent with the idea of mindfulness, noticing your emotions without judging them can help promote acceptance. Mostly, everything is going well, so you have every reason to be happy. Furthermore, accepting the fact that nothing is ever perfect can allow you to notice the brief obstacle to your happiness without becoming devastated.
  5. Taking context into account. Thinking about your social, cultural, and systemic contexts becomes the last step in the path to happiness. This might be a tall order, but not if you break it down. While out with friends, you obviously wish to be happy, and the situation is set up to achieve just that (minus the potentially annoying comment). But sometimes the situation isn’t one that can, or even should, foster happiness. Would you regard it as appropriate to be happy if you saw something that disturbed you during the event? Maybe your eye flickers across the room to a television screen showing a wildfire that had gotten out of control. Or perhaps the conversation shifts to social problems that have been of great concern to you. Rather than shove that out of awareness, accept that life has its imperfections, which can impinge upon your own mood.

Taking the Happiness Pathway to Heart

As the authors conclude, despite the universality of happiness as a goal, many people “find ways to fumble it." Taking the middle road between pitfalls and promises within each of these five steps can help you ensure that you’ll keep the fumbling to a minimum.

It’s also important to differentiate between the components of happiness, which include eudaimonia (finding meaning and purpose), evaluation (satisfaction), and affect (feelings of pleasure). There may be times when you feel what you’re doing is fulfilling your sense of purpose even though it’s painful at the moment. You might also feel contentment rather than joy as you reflect on broader themes of your life. Happiness doesn’t always have to equal ecstasy.

To sum up, the pursuit of happiness can be paved with promise rather than pitfalls, especially if you know how to capitalize on the strategies that will help you keep your eye on your long-term goals.

*Fans of the musical Wicked will undoubtedly recognize this quote from "Dancing Through Life."

item.title: Evil Deeds and Dangerous States of Mind
item.description:
Psychosis

Evil Deeds and Dangerous States of Mind

Why the insanity defense is complicated, uncommon, and so difficult to prove.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • The insanity defense relies on the defendant's mental state at the time of the crime, not at trial.
  • Psychosis is unpredictable, with biological and non-biological triggers that can strike at any stage of life.
  • The case illustrates the challenge of proving a defendant's prior mental state beyond a reasonable doubt.

This is Part 2 of a series about the Lindsay Clancy case. Read Part 1 here.

The so-called insanity defense, or LCR (lack of criminal responsibility) as it is called in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, differs from determining a defendant's competency to stand trial, which is about their current mental status. Instead, it hinges on the defendant's state of mind at the moment the crime was committed, which, in some cases, can be years or even decades ago. When conducting forensic evaluations for the insanity defense, determining (or trying to reconstruct) the defendant's state of mind before, during, and immediately following the criminal offense is absolutely essential. What was Ms. Clancy's condition during this time period? Perhaps most crucially, was she psychotic?

Source: Ken Lund/CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons

What is Psychosis?

Psychosis is the most debilitating of all psychiatric disorders. If truth be told, no one really knows where psychosis comes from or what causes it. Psychosis appears to have some genetic basis and can run in families, though this is not always the case. And though the chance of identical (monozygotic) twins raised in similar or the same environments both suffering from a psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia is fairly high (up to 50 percent to 70 percent), it is still not 100 percent, indicating there are other significant factors beyond biology and genetics at play. Some of those factors are psychological stress, substance abuse, and emotional trauma. I have worked with psychotic patients for many years, and it's clear that there is a significant psychological component to this complex and devastating mental state and that it is an archetypal human experience to which none of us is totally immune. The frightening fact of the matter is that people can become psychotic with or without a genetic history of the disorder and at any stage of life, especially during periods of extreme biopsychosocial stress.

What Was Clancy's State of Mind at the Time of the Killings?

For me, the key question here has to do with whether or not the defendant was psychotic at the time she committed the killings. Most of the mental health professionals who evaluated Ms. Clancy, including her treating psychiatrist, did not note any psychotic signs or symptoms during the period prior to the offense. Nor does she seem to exhibit psychotic symptomatology at present. However, one forensic psychologist who treated her at a hospital following the crime diagnosed her as suffering from both postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder, stating that she feared others could hear her thoughts, a classic psychotic symptom called "thought broadcasting." The assertion that, according to another forensic psychologist who evaluated her after her arrest, Ms. Clancy told him, her hospital chaplain, and her husband about having heard a persistent disembodied male voice commanding her to kill her kids and herself before doing so, something clinically called a "command hallucination," is certainly possible but also somewhat suspicious. Malingering or lying about such things would not be unusual in such a high-stakes case.

It is essential to keep in mind that Lindsay Clancy was an experienced labor and delivery nurse, had almost certainly seen postpartum and other kinds of psychosis before, and conceivably may have realized that unless she could convince the jury that she experienced psychotic symptoms such as command hallucinations, it would be considerably more challenging for her lawyers to prevail. (This is especially true under Massachusetts law, which requires the state to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that she was not too debilitated by her mental state to be held criminally responsible.)

It would now appear that the lone juror who forced Ms. Clancy's mistrial did so because he apparently believed that the prosecution had sufficiently demonstrated the defendant's guilt and criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt, rejecting the defense team's claim of lack of criminal responsibility (LCR). This seems a reasonable position, especially if the defendant was not convincingly shown to be psychotic at the time of the crime. On the other hand, if Ms. Clancy was telling the truth about having experienced command hallucinations and thought broadcasting before or during the commission of this offense, that would have proved sufficient to win her case in my opinion. So this is, for me, a central point. Time will tell—if there is another trial.

From what has been publicly reported, it sounds as though, at the very least, Ms. Clancy suffered from severe depressive symptoms before, during, and immediately after the killings, when she attempted to commit suicide by superficially slashing her wrists and neck and then jumping out of a two-story window, causing her to become paralyzed from the waist down. (This appears to have been more of a legitimate attempt than a manipulative suicide gesture, though it is highly likely that a registered nurse like Clancy would know how to cut their wrists if they really wanted to die.) Prior to the murders, she had evidently consulted numerous clinicians, including psychiatrists, psychotherapists, and psychiatric nurse practitioners, regarding symptoms such as acute insomnia, sadness, and anxiety, had been briefly psychiatrically hospitalized, and was prescribed numerous psychotropic medications intended to ameliorate her symptoms.

According to her mother, who is also a nurse but not a mental health professional, Ms. Clancy was "paranoid" during this period, but it is not clear what she meant by this. Clinically, this term paranoia refers to paranoid delusions or fixed, irrational beliefs, which, if they were indeed present around and during the time of the murders, would support the argument that Clancy was psychotic. But this was not emphasized at trial. Did Clancy become delusional during that period? By definition, true paranoia includes paranoid delusions of some sort, e.g., the patient fearing the CIA, FBI, etc., is spying on them or that people in general are against them and trying to deliberately harm or trick them. Ms. Clancy's reported fear of sleeping alone or that her psychiatric medications were "destroying her mind" does not, in and of itself, rise to the definition of clinical paranoia, by definition, a psychotic symptom. There was also some evidence presented indicating that she had probably been thinking of killing her children and perhaps herself for some time, citing searches on her computer or phone asking, for instance, whether the airbags in her car could be disabled and how to locate the carotid artery.

Conclusion

In most insanity cases here in California, which, unlike in Massachusetts, need to be proven by the defense by a preponderance of the evidence, a lower bar, rather than beyond a reasonable doubt, without more convincing proof of the presence of psychotic symptoms such as delusions or auditory, visual, or other hallucinations, it seems unlikely to me that a jury would find that the severe symptoms of depression and anxiety alone, though clearly painful, were sufficiently debilitating to impair a defendant's reality testing, insight, and judgment to the point of being unable to appreciate the criminality or wrongfulness of their conduct or to have been, as a result of said mental disease or defect, unable to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law, as required in Massachusetts. Suicide is one thing. Filicide is another. For a mother to calculatingly and coldly strangle her own children to death and be excused, acquitted, or found not guilty for doing so by a jury of her peers requires, it seems to me, a higher burden of proof.

item.title: Commemorating 9/11, Celebrating 9/12
item.description:
Optimism

Commemorating 9/11, Celebrating 9/12

Personal Perspective: Let's honor the 25th anniversary with courageous optimism.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • Celebrating the unity of 9/12 can help Americans process what seems like unrecoverable loss from tragedy.
  • Recapturing 9/12's spirit means choosing service, hope, and unity over cynicism and division.
  • Those in uniformed service lead by example as they pass the torch to the next generation of courageous heroes.

Twenty-five years have come and gone since that cool, clear September morning when evil tried to break the spirit of America, yet the memories of 9/11 make it feel like it was just yesterday. While so much has changed—in my life, the lives of so many others, and the world around us since that day—so much has also stayed the same. I still smell the smells, still hear the sounds, and still see things my mind has not and will never be able to unsee.

This week, as we gather once again to honor the 2,977 souls lost and the thousands more who have perished since from related illnesses, we must do more than simply remember the tragedy of 9/11. We must embrace the strength, unity, and hope of 9/12—the day that showed the world what America truly stands for.

The courageous optimism of 9/11's first responders

I still get emotional when I think and talk about 9/11. The details may have become as fuzzy as my pictures over the decades, but the sounds, smells, and tastes of that day remain forever imprinted on my soul. What defines me today, however, is not the darkness of September 11th, but the light that emerged on September 12th—a light that must guide us toward the future our nation deserves.

The first responders who ran into the towers when everyone else was running out embodied what I call courageous optimism. These police officers and firefighters made a conscious choice—driven by self-determination and self-efficacy, an unwavering belief that they possessed the skill sets necessary to effect positive outcomes for those still trapped inside. They didn't run toward danger out of reckless abandon, but with the optimistic conviction that their training, experience, and dedication could make the difference between life and death for innocent Americans. Their courage wasn't born from naïveté about the dangers they faced, but from an optimistic faith in their ability to save lives, even against impossible odds. They did not act without fear, but rather despite it.

Today's first responders carry forward this same tradition of courageous optimism. They put on their uniforms each day knowing the evil they may face but believing in their power to do good. They are the modern sheepdogs, keeping wolves at bay not just with strength and skill, but with unshakeable optimism that their service creates a safer, better world, embodied in the oath they took.

What we learned from 9/12

I remember September 12, 2001, when flags flew from every home, business, and street corner. We were truly "one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all." We didn't see each other as members of competing political ideologies or different demographics. We were simply Americans—unhyphenated Americans—united in purpose and strengthened by shared values. That unity wasn't weakness disguised as strength; it was strength revealing itself through compassion, resilience, and unwavering hope for tomorrow, serving a purpose greater than ourselves.

In the years since, we've allowed divisive forces to fracture what 9/12 built. We've forgotten that our Constitution—the same document that grants us the right to challenge it—was forged by people who understood that unity doesn't mean uniformity, and that strength comes from our ability to stand together despite our differences.

The lesson of 9/12 for today's first responders: Your service matters not just for what you prevent, but for what you inspire. When you respond to a call, you're not just addressing an immediate crisis—you're demonstrating that America still believes in protecting the innocent, serving others before ourselves, and maintaining hope even in the darkest moments. You are leading by example while earning your badge every day.

9/11's legacy

To the young men and women beginning careers in uniformed service, you are inheriting a legacy of courageously optimistic heroes who came before you. Those who served on 9/11 and in the decades since have handed you tools forged in the fires of that terrible day—tools of resilience, dedication, and unshakeable faith in America's capacity for good. Use them wisely. Use them with hope. Use them to protect your mental health, so that you can serve with the best version of yourself.

As we remember those who answered the call 25 years ago and in the days, weeks, and years that followed—many of whom continue to suffer physically and emotionally—we must ask ourselves: How do we honor their sacrifice? Not through perpetual anger or endless division, not by platforming those who speak ill of America, but by recapturing the spirit of 9/12. By choosing optimism over cynicism, unity over fragmentation, and service over self-interest.

History teaches us that those who forget the past are doomed to repeat it. But history also shows us that those who remember the best of their past can build an even better, stronger future. The courageous optimism of our 9/11 first responders and the national unity of 9/12 must be our north star as we move forward—not as painful memories to preserve, but as living principles to practice.

This September 11th, after we've honored the fallen and thanked the heroes, let us commit to making every day feel like 9/12. Let us be proud Americans who choose love over hate, service over selfishness, and unity over division. For that is the legacy that best honors those who made the ultimate sacrifice, and the foundation upon which we can build a more peaceful world for generations to come.

The towers fell, but America's spirit rose. That spirit—that courageous optimism—must always prevail, for we are “the land of the free and the home of the brave.”

item.title: 3 Reasons We Miss Lovers We Would Never Want Back
item.description:
Relationships

3 Reasons We Miss Lovers We Would Never Want Back

You can miss someone deeply and still know you should never be with them again.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • Missing an ex is not the same as wanting a reunion.
  • A person's attractive qualities may differ from their suitability as a long-term partner.
  • Separation can intensify longing even when familiarity had diminished romantic passion.
  • Love and life sometimes conflict, making separation the wiser choice.

Why do we sometimes long for someone we would never choose to live with again?

Romantic and sexual intensity are often fueled by novelty and change, and they tend to fade with familiarity. Yet separation can produce a curious reversal. We may miss someone we know extremely well, even crave seeing them again, while having little desire to rebuild a lasting relationship with them. This apparent paradox stems from three factors: We idealize the past, we confuse a desirable person with a compatible partner, and love does not always fit the life we need to live.

1. We Idealize the Past

"When I look at my wife now, after 40 years of marriage, I still see the young and beautiful girl I first met." —A man

Longing for a former lover often has a utopian quality. We are drawn not only to what once existed, but also to what we wish had existed. Memory and imagination can create a version of the past that is more attractive than reality ever was.

Idealization leads us to focus on what was wonderful while overlooking what made the relationship difficult or unsustainable. Unlike a real relationship, an imagined one requires no compromises, negotiations, disappointments, or everyday frustrations. Such positive illusions are common in romantic love. We often minimize a partner's shortcomings while magnifying their virtues. In this sense, we may fall in love not only with a real person but also with our imagined version of that person. After a breakup, this tendency can become even stronger. Ironically, research suggests that excessive idealization may undermine relationship quality, contributing to lower satisfaction and greater jealousy and infidelity (Ventura-León et al., 2025).

Distance removes many of the conflicts that once characterized the relationship, leaving vivid memories of intimacy, excitement, affection, and sexual attraction. An ex-lover can therefore appear far more appealing in memory than in everyday reality. Moderate positive illusions can enrich romantic life. Yet when longing rests primarily on an idealized reconstruction of the past, it may reveal more about our imagination than about what we would actually want to experience again.

2. A Desirable Person Is Not Necessarily a Compatible Partner

"I love you not only for what you are, but for what I am when I am with you." —Elizabeth Barrett Browning

We evaluate romantic partners in at least two ways. First, we assess their individual qualities: How attractive, intelligent, kind, humorous, or passionate are they? Second, we assess their relational value: How well do we function together?

Source: RDNE Stock Project/Pexels

These two dimensions often diverge. Intelligence is generally attractive, yet a large intellectual gap can create distance between partners. A strong sexual appetite may be appealing, but major differences in sexual needs can generate ongoing tension. Someone may possess many admirable qualities and still be poorly suited as a long-term partner for a particular person. Conversely, two imperfect individuals may create an exceptional relationship because they bring out the best in each other.

This distinction helps explain why we may miss an ex without wanting to reunite. After separation, we often remember, and sometimes exaggerate, a former partner's personal qualities: their beauty, humor, sexuality, vitality, warmth, or intelligence. What fades from view is the relational dimension: how well we actually worked together. Personal qualities dominate initial attraction. Over time, compatibility becomes increasingly important. We discover whether our values, personalities, expectations, and lifestyles genuinely fit. An ex may therefore remain highly desirable as a person while being unsuitable as a partner. This is one reason longing can survive even after we recognize that the relationship needed to end.

3. Love and Life Do Not Always Pull in the Same Direction

"There is love, of course. And then there's life, its enemy." —Jean Anouilh

One of the most painful romantic decisions is leaving someone we still love. We need love to flourish, but profound love also requires a life that can sustain it. This raises a difficult question: Should we remain in a relationship that undermines other important aspects of well-being simply because we still love the person?

Romantic compromises often involve sacrificing some romantic value, such as passion, intimacy, or excitement, in order to preserve other important values, including psychological well-being, personal freedom, family stability, security, or professional fulfillment. Such compromises reflect a fundamental reality: We are finite beings. We cannot always realize all our romantic ideals while simultaneously achieving every major life goal. Flourishing often requires flexibility and acceptance of something different from what we originally desired.

Popular culture encourages the belief that love conquers all. Reality is more complicated. Life can impose constraints that romantic feelings alone cannot overcome. Recognizing this acknowledges that love is one important component of a flourishing life, not its sole component (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019). This helps explain a puzzling experience. We may leave someone we still love and continue longing for them long afterward. The decision may have been right for our lives even while the longing remains true to our hearts.

Longing Is Not the Same as Wanting Someone Back

"Nothing burns like an old flame." —Harlan Coben

"I am not really in love with my ex, but I am definitely still heartbroken." —A woman

Romantic love does not exist in isolation. It is embedded in shared habits, expectations, compromises, and ways of living. When people long for an ex, they often focus on the emotional and sexual intensity of the relationship while neglecting the realities that once made it difficult. In memory, the person becomes separated from the incompatibilities, disappointments, conflicts, and practical challenges that contributed to the breakup. For this reason, longing should not be confused with a desire for reunion. Indeed, attempts to rekindle a former relationship may sometimes intensify rather than relieve breakup distress (Eisma et al., 2022).

There is also a deeper paradox. Familiarity often diminishes intensity within an ongoing relationship, whereas separation can revive longing for the very same person. Distance can make someone emotionally vivid precisely because they are no longer woven into everyday life. What we miss may be the person we were with them, the excitement this person inspired, or even the relationship we hoped to create but never achieved. None of these necessarily means we want to build a future together. Enduring romantic love requires more than longing. It requires compatibility, mutual responsiveness, shared growth, and the capacity to build a meaningful life together.

Sometimes, then, the most honest conclusion is also the most paradoxical: "I miss you. I still desire you. I still cherish something about what we had. But I do not want you back." Longing can preserve the emotional value of a relationship without demonstrating that the relationship should be restored.

item.title: College Students May Face Greater AI Risks Than Children
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

College Students May Face Greater AI Risks Than Children

At 18, the law says you're finished. The prefrontal cortex disagrees.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • The prefrontal cortex is not fully mature until the mid-20s, well past the legal threshold of adulthood.
  • At 18, legal protections end, but neurological vulnerability to AI remains high.
  • Universities are the last chance to build cognitive protections before true adulthood.

I have spent the last year building a case for protecting children from the worst effects of AI in schools. Whether that’s age restrictions, usage policies, tool limits, etc., the entire apparatus assumes the danger is greater for the younger users and decreases as the child matures toward adolescence. By 18, these protections are largely removed because the law determines you are now an adult. Thus, you're now on your own.

How Brain Development Continues Beyond Age 18

The developmental science says the opposite. The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain responsible for planning, impulse control, and weighing long-term consequences, is not fully mature until the mid-20s. This is the region needed for the kind of independent decision-making and thinking a university education is supposed to build: synthesis, evaluation, judgment, and the capacity to hold two competing ideas and navigate the nuance.

Thus, the window for building higher-order cognitive capabilities begins in childhood, but continues through the 20s. Knoll and colleagues trained 633 people on relational reasoning and found that 16- to 18-year-olds improved nearly twice as much as younger adolescents. So while it may often seem sound that 18 is the end of the developmental story, this is the year when the construction is running the hardest.

Challenges for College Students With Still-Developing Reasoning Skills

Now consider what a 19-year-old college student today is being asked to do with that still-forming equipment. Construct an argument. Defend it. Read in depth a new domain of content. Make connections. Form relationships with others. Much of this, if not all, a large language model will be able to imitate on request in some capacity. The student offloads the thesis, the weighing of right vs. wrong, and the construction of her arguments, and receives something that she feels is her work. But verification isn’t authorship. The brain that would have built the capability through both success and failure over time does not receive the practice. And because this is the peak period for building those reasoning skills and judgment, what is missed is really a portion of the future self.

There is a second, more invisible, problem running underneath, and it’s more difficult for a developing mind to notice. Steinberg described something called the developmental imbalance. The limbic system, which drives reward-seeking, matures ahead of the prefrontal system that regulates it. This shows during the late teens and early 20s, when the pull toward the faster, easier, more immediately satisfying option is at its neurological peak. The ability to resist that pull is still catching up. AI is the fastest, easiest, most immediately satisfying option for nearly any cognitive task a student faces. The mismatch does not make students lazy, but it does make the outsourcing neurologically difficult to refuse.

Why Young Adults Need Protection from AI Overuse

For university students, developmental windows remain open, and reasoning capacity is under peak construction. The brain's own reward system is pushing toward the path of least resistance. And at 18, every piece of protective architecture—the teacher who oversees tasks, the parent who manages the screen time, the school policy that governs AI, the technology platforms with age restrictions—are all withdrawn at once.

Foremen don’t withdraw scaffolding from a building while concrete is still being laid. Doctors don’t remove a cast before the bone has set and healed. But somehow, it has been normalized to remove developmental safeguards when you turn 18, when the prefrontal cortex is doing its most consequential work, and hand her an AI tool that can simply do that work for her.

The 14-year-old who uses AI irresponsibly has adults around him who can intervene. The 22-year-old is often alone, and he needs that protection as well.

I’m not advising we restrict college students the same way we restrict children. I’m arguing that we need to recognize that the developmental consequences of AI on cognition do not end at high school graduation. Universities are the last structured environment most young people pass through. What they choose to protect in those years, and what they choose to let a tool interfere with, will shape a generation's capacity in how they approach solving problems.

The developmental framework behind this argument is set out in Before the Window Closes, a policy brief written with Bassem Nasir.

item.title: Can Bad People Make Beautiful Art?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Can Bad People Make Beautiful Art?

The morality of the maker affects how viewers experience their art.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • Aesthetic evaluations change depending on the context in which the art is viewed, a study shows.
  • Art by a morally bad person elicits more negative and fewer positive emotions than art by a virtuous person.
  • People with greater art experience are especially sensitive to information about an artist's values.
Source: Isabella Bobrow

Co-authored by Isabella Bobrow

Last week, we collectively mourned several great artists. One such legend was Dolly Parton, often cited as the most-liked person in America. Her philanthropic efforts, support of new artists, and positive outlook cemented her legacy as one of the icons of American music. Two days later, the art world was struck again by news of the loss of Yayoi Kusama, a visionary painter, sculptor, and performance artist who became one of the most famous female fine artists in history.

As Kusama tributes flooded the internet, so did criticism because of her past racist writings. In her 2002 autobiography and previous writings, Kusama made racist, crude, and sexualized characterizations of Black people. When this pattern was brought to light in 2023, she addressed it in a statement in The San Francisco Chronicle, saying, “I deeply regret using hurtful and offensive language in my book.” Many have not accepted this apology.

We often reckon with how to engage with the works of creators whose private actions we disagree with. Do Tesla owners need to disclose that they like the car but don’t agree with Elon Musk’s promotion of far-right politics? Should Harry Potter fans burn their books over JK Rowling’s transphobic comments? Should one stop listening to Ye, formerly Kanye West, after his antisemitic tirades? These aren’t just thought experiments. Most artists make their living by selling their work; a change in public perception can have damning consequences.

Research study

In a recently published study, our lab tested this age-old question: Can people separate the art from the artist?1 Do we perceive something as less beautiful because it was made by a person whose values we find ugly?

Aesthetic evaluations do not exist in a vacuum. They are affected by contextual factors, including the venue in which we encounter the art, titles of the work, our knowledge of art history, and our cultural background. Additionally, perceived value, intentionality, and assessment of authenticity can make a difference in our experience.2,3,4 Is the moral character of the artist one such factor that modulates appreciation of their work?

To determine if moral information influences aesthetic evaluations, we randomly paired famous morally good and bad people with amateur paintings. For example, some participants saw an artwork paired with a short description of beloved childhood TV star Fred Rogers. Others saw the same artwork paired with a biography of Ted Bundy, the notorious serial killer.

What we found

The results confirmed the idea that we incorporate artists’ moral values when we view their art. When paired with the “bad” artists, people liked the artworks less and found them less beautiful. They were more likely to feel negative emotions (challenged, angry, upset) and less likely to feel positive emotions (calm, enraptured, interested, etc.) than people who saw the same art paired with a morally virtuous person.

One unexpected finding was that the more experience viewers had engaging with aesthetics, the more moral values affected how edified, enlightened, or inspired they felt in response to the art. People with greater exposure to the arts are influenced disproportionately by this kind of value-based contextual information. This finding contrasts with the observation that people less engaged with aesthetics are influenced disproportionately by art-historical information.5 People with more prior art experience are less affected by factual information and more affected by value information.

Implications

Our results do not mean that artists are less moral than anyone else. It's just that they're visible when they misstep, whether the transgression is a social media spat or an affiliation with someone like Jeffrey Epstein. The results do tell us that, even though we perceptually discriminate between different objects easily, we are not very good at disentangling our moral and aesthetic values.

Perhaps not all press is good press. In addition to changing how we feel about a work of art, knowledge about its creator’s morals and (un)ethical behaviors can make the work appear more or less beautiful. For fans of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity Mirrors, staring into the abyss could be unsettling once one learns of her anti-Black sentiments. Flaws in the landscape become impossible to ignore when reflected endlessly, forcing us to reckon with a complicated image. Kusama’s artwork makes explicit what is true about every aesthetic encounter—they reflect us, along with our biases, knowledge, and values.

item.title: Lessons From 'I'm Still Here: A Cat's Purpose Forever'
item.description:
Grief

Lessons From 'I'm Still Here: A Cat's Purpose Forever'

In her new book, Cathryn Michon offers comfort to cat lovers navigating loss.

Posted September 5, 2026

Key points
  • In "I'm Still Here," Cathryn Michon aims to help people realize that a cat's love never dies.
  • Highly inspirational, the book is not about grief, but rather a return to joy.
  • Michon highlights how cats are great spiritual teachers, bringing wisdom and a unique presence to human lives.
Source: Foto Panda/Pexels.

Our companion animals—cats, dogs, and many others—are amazing beings. For many human guardians, they are forever present, even after the transition to the other side, and it's essential to love them when they're alive and afterwards. Writer E.B. Bartels calls this forever grief "good grief."

Two years ago, I interviewed the eclectic Cathryn Michon about her book, I'm Still Here: A Dog's Purpose Forever, from which I and many others learned a lot about grief, death, and dying. Now, I'm pleased to interview Michon once again about her new book, beautifully illustrated by Michele Dettering, I’m Still Here: A Cat's Purpose Forever.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write I'm Still Here: A Cat's Purpose Forever?

Cathryn Michon: I am known for making movies about dogs as a writer of A Dog's Purpose, as well as a writer, director, and producer of the upcoming Netflix movie A Dog's Perfect Christmas, but I was a cat lover first. It seems like media in general pays a lot more attention to dogs than cats, and in some small way, I hope this book comforts feline lovers like me who are dealing with the loss of a cat. It's the hardest thing we can experience, but I truly do believe that their love is still here—we just need to open our hearts to it.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

CM: I hope that people who are having trouble processing the loss of their cat will find their way to this book. It’s a gentle collection of free-verse poetry and beautiful watercolor art that celebrates the feline spirit and offers comfort during an incredibly difficult time.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

CM: This book is like no other because it is a direct message from an angel cat, letting you know that she is still here, watching you and loving you, even as she now runs free with all the souls you have ever lost. But it’s so much more than that, because this angel cat wants to confirm what you may have already suspected: Cats are smarter than we are capable of understanding, and they basically run everything, whether you want them to or not.

Don’t worry, just because you’re not as spiritually wise as your cat doesn’t mean that they don’t love you. Quite the opposite, actually. They find your general cluelessness endlessly adorable.

One of the other messages this angel cat wants you to really take away is that your relationship is eternal. But that’s true for every soul you have ever loved; we are all eternal beings. As my husband, W. Bruce Cameron, author of A Dog’s Purpose, points out in his preface to this book, the first law of thermodynamics confirms that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it only changes form. So, of course, that must apply to the most potent form of energy in all creation: love. Love is forever.

Source: Cathryn Michon.

But I should also mention that, with this angel cat’s extremely high level of self-esteem about what she refers to as “the natural superiority of cats in general and me specifically,” this cat is pretty funny. That’s an aspect of the book that early reviewers have really enjoyed. This cat is funny because, well… cats are funny.

But mostly, her message is that you, and all the cats you have loved, are forever. And when we part on Earth, what cats most want is for you to get another cat. As far as cats are concerned, they make you a better human. Honestly, I agree with this angel cat on that one.

I wrote this book primarily for those who believe as I do and are seeking comfort for themselves or for a friend who has lost a beloved animal companion. When you don’t know what to say to a friend who is grieving, this book—with its tender, gentle message and stunning art—can bring relief. That’s what happened with my book I’m Still Here: A Dog’s Purpose Forever, and I really hope this book gives that same comfort, and even joy, to cat lovers.

I have given my other book to so many friends who have lost a dog, and it feels so good to give a friend the exact message they are aching to hear.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

CM: There simply isn't another hardcover book out there that combines free-verse poetry and original watercolor art, printed on textured watercolor paper, to create such a beautiful gift for a grieving friend—or an object of comfort that you give yourself.

It's beautiful to the eyes and to the touch. It's specifically designed with a watercolor front leaf page, perfect for placing a photograph of your own angel cat and writing a dedication to their memory. I believe that in an increasingly digital world, a lushly printed book is the perfect way to honor the memory of someone you loved.

Many people use my books as the foundation of a memory corner, and I'm so proud of that.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about the fascinating lives of cats, they will come to treat them with more respect and dignity?

CM: As a longtime animal advocate, I am always hopeful that people will treat all animals with respect and dignity. But this book is a celebration of cats as our loving companions and family members. We owe them our loving care because we have largely removed them from the natural circle of life in which they were predators.

A key component of that care is kindly helping them cross over the Rainbow Bridge when that is the most compassionate choice. This cat wants you to know that they understand what is happening when you help them, and they are grateful.

As humans, we can’t generally make that decision for other humans because it’s complicated by money and other concerns. But when you help a pet cross over, that is a decision made out of pure love, and I believe with all my heart that our pets know it.
